public_rationale: Marcus wrote on December 13, 2025 that among American AI companies, a lead 'never lasts for more than a few months.' The contract tests this on the Arena overall leaderboard from May 2023 to the post date. It reads 'a few months' as about five or six months at most. Ars Technica reported on March 27, 2024 that versions of OpenAI's GPT-4 had stayed at the top of Chatbot Arena from about May 10, 2023 until Claude 3 Opus passed them on March 26, 2024 (e1). That is about ten and a half months, which meets the contract's contradiction condition. Later reports put Gemini 2.5 Pro at #1 on March 26, 2025 (e2), GPT-5 on August 7, 2025 (e3), and Gemini 3 Pro on November 18, 2025 (e4). Those reports are about four and a half and three and a half months apart. They do not show whether #1 changed hands between them. A claim that says 'never' fails if one run is clearly longer, and e1 reports such a run.
limitations: The leaderboard dates come from news reports, not from an official Arena history of every change at #1.
The 2025 reports give the dates when models took #1. They do not show how long each model stayed there or whether #1 changed hands in between.
Top positions are sometimes within error margins, and the reports do not address ties.
Other capability measures, or market-share measures, might show leads of different lengths.
If 'never' was meant to cover only the recent period, the evidence used here does not settle that narrower reading.

statement.excerpt: (You can see the same dynamic within the American companies, where a lead never lasts for more than a few months).
statement.document_title: The core misconception that is driving American AI policy

from_speaker: for more than a few months
our_interpretation: 'Lead' means holding the top capability spot among US AI labs, measured here by the Arena (formerly Chatbot Arena/LMArena) overall text leaderboard, the most widely cited public ranking.
'Never' covers the generative AI race from the launch of public leaderboards (May 2023) up to the post date.
'A few months' is read as roughly up to five or six months; a run of ten months or more clearly exceeds it.
criteria.support_condition: Every US lab's run at #1 on the main leaderboard from 2023 to December 2025 lasted no more than a few months.
criteria.contradiction_condition: At least one US lab held #1 for clearly more than a few months (e.g., most of a year) during that period.
